hansard.speaker: Baroness Benjamin (LD)
hansard.text: My Lords, I thank the Minister for her Answer. The Government have said that AI developers must report a breach within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, but in Australia OpenAI did not become aware that its agent had broken into the Medicare system until two months later. OpenAI says that its agent broke in without being asked to do so. Would a similar intrusion into the NHS have to be reported? If an AI agent hacks the NHS system on its own, who would the Government hold criminally responsible? Also, the reporting duty covers only personal data that risks harming individuals. The cyber security and resilience Bill's 24-hour rule applies to regulated organisations, not AI developers. hansard.debate: Creative Industries, Culture and the Arts
hansard.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, it is a pleasure and a privilege to be leading this debate. I declare my interests as chair of Camden STEAM and as a trustee of the Maltings arts, heritage and community centre in Wells-next-the-Sea, Norfolk. I begin by taking us back to 1997. A Labour Government were elected, with my noble friend Lord Smith of Finsbury—one of my heroes and in his place—as Secretary of State for the newly named Department for Culture, Media and Sport. A bold and inspired step was taken: a globally recognised world first, the defining of the creative industries as “those industries which have their origin in individual creativity, skill and talent and which have a potential for wealth and job creation through the generation and exploitation of intellectual property”. It was followed by supporting policies, including the first tax reliefs for the film industry. At that time, the sector employed around 1.4 million people and generated some £60 million a year in value added. Today, the scale of the sector and its growth are extraordinary. The creative industries contribute over £160 billion in GVA, accounting for 5.6% of the UK economy and growing more than twice as fast as the wider economy since 2010. They support 2.4 million jobs, representing around 7% of UK employment, with a further 1.3 million people working in creative occupations across other sectors. The UK is second only to the United States in creative exports, generating around £70 billion annually, and remains one of the world's most attractive destinations for inward investment and cultural tourism. hansard.debate: Creative Industries, Culture and the Arts
hansard.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross (CB)
hansard.text: My Lords, I too am grateful to the noble Baroness, Lady Caine of Kentish Town, for securing this debate and opening it with such brio. Noble Lords have heard much about the development of a UK sovereign AI model. It would be based on licensed data we can trust and would be an “open weight” model, so that it could be adapted by British commercial companies and public bodies, customised for local needs—and, of course, would help the creative industries in the process. Crucially, it would not need to store its data in data centres outside this country. The Government have put £120 million into such a fund, and it is in the British commercial interest to take it forward. However, what would make a British AI model exceptional and build trust among an anxious public is if universities, public organisations—such as the British Library—and public service broadcasters, especially the BBC, were involved to ensure that its development incorporated public service values. The UN has already developed red lines for new AI models, most of which have been rejected by the present US Administration, but we in this country could develop a British AI model that would hold to the principles of controlling online harm, protecting our children online, and ensuring that it would not be misused by bad actors. The involvement of the BBC would help develop this model and communicate its benefits through trusted channels. The BBC has been at the forefront of technological advance for decades. hansard.speaker: Bobby Dean

However, just because the consumer may be compensated, it does not mean that we should lose sight of the crime. The victim still suffers the trauma, and the criminal still keeps the money. The new clause focuses on the unfairness of UK financial firms being left alone on the hook for compensation when the vast majority of APP fraud originates on US-based online platforms, which not only facilitate the crime but make hundreds of millions of pounds in ad revenue from it. We must change that financial incentive. We want to give the FCA the rule-making power to ensure that the tech companies are liable for the cost of reimbursing APP fraud victims. hansard.speaker: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (Baroness Lloyd of Effra) (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, AI developers should keep their systems under safe control. We expect prompt, transparent reporting of unexpected behaviour. In respect of breach of systems, the Computer Misuse Act applies to AI developers, and they must not breach systems. If breaches happen, victims should be informed immediately. If personal data, such as NHS records, is accessed, the Information Commission should be informed within 72 hours. The cyber Bill strengthens protections for essential services such as NHS trusts. Regulated AI services must report significant loss of control incidents within 24 hours.

hansard.speaker: Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath (Lab)
hansard.text: In January 2026, the DfE published product safety standards for generative AI in education which outline the capabilities and features that products and systems should need to meet to be considered safe for users in educational settings. The statutory guidance Keeping Children Safe i n Education makes it clear that schools and colleges should do all they reasonably can to limit children's exposure to harmful content, including having appropriate filtering and monitoring systems in place. We are clear that the unsafe use of technology in schools is not acceptable. Schools and colleges have a statutory responsibility to keep children and young people safe, online as well as offline. To help them achieve that, we have published product safety standards for generative AI in education, which will support schools and colleges to understand which products are safe in education and support edtech providers to design safe products.

hansard.speaker: Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath (Lab)
hansard.text: I wonder whether that suggests something about the noble Lord's music tastes. Evidence shows that edtech can support teaching and learning, pupil outcomes, inclusion and teacher workload, but impact varies by technology and context. The DfE's Technology in Schools survey provides nationally representative evidence on schools' use of technology and AI, the benefits and the barriers to effective implementation. The Education Endowment Foundation's evidence base highlights the importance of pedagogy and effective implementation in determining the impact of digital technology. Evidence on newer technologies, particularly AI-enabled personalised learning, remains mixed and developing. We are keeping a close watch on the results of all that research, including on inclusion, as the noble Lord suggests.

hansard.speaker: Baroness Brinton (LD)
hansard.text: My Lords, my noble friend's Question covered the NHS and personal data but, of course, various government departments have plenty of personal data about citizens elsewhere. The National Cyber Security Centre's Annual Review 2025 noted a sharp escalation in significant incidents. hansard.debate: Creative Industries, Culture and the Arts
hansard.speaker: Baroness Keeley (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, I congratulate my noble friend Lady McAnea on her maiden speech and my noble friend Lady Caine on securing this debate on the creative industries, and the brilliant way she opened it. The creative industries are one of the UK's great success stories. The music industry is central to that success, contributing £8.4 billion in GVA, generating £5 billion in exports and employing more than 220,000 people. To ensure that that growth continues and reaches every part of the country, the Government should focus on three clear priorities. First, we must address the threat posed by AI and copyright infringement. The Communications and Digital Select Committee report highlighted the danger that generative AI presents to creators' livelihoods. I urge the Government to implement the committee's recommendations, particularly by rejecting any commercial text- and data-mining exception, introducing protections against unauthorised digital replicas, and legislating for transparency. Secondly, we must invest in music education. Currently, the music industry is living on the legacy of the much stronger music education we had in the past. Changing this means rebuilding music education in state schools. Entries for GCSE and A-level music have been declining since 2010. Reversing this trend requires more specialist music teachers and the most effective step towards achieving that would be restoring the music teacher training bursary. As we come up to the work on the curriculum review, I also urge Ministers to champion the arts and music as the valuable subjects to learn and teach that we know they are. hansard.speaker: Lord Markham (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, my experience as Health Minister of dealing with the cyber attack on NHS diagnostic facilities reinforced the importance of minimising the amount of identifiable patient data held across different systems. Given the increasing capabilities of autonomous AI agents, what steps are the Government taking to ensure that NHS data is anonymised or pseudonymised wherever possible so that, even if unauthorised access occurs, the risk to individual patients is significantly reduced? This is not a matter of GDPR; all GDPR regulations are followed in these cases. It is a matter of the NHS protecting our data by not making it identifiable.

hansard.speaker: Baroness Lloyd of Effra (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, as the noble Baroness says, the Bill sets out duties for essential services to manage their risks to their systems. Where an AI digital service, such as a cloud computing service, falls within scope, it will have to follow those reporting duties. This includes notifying regulators of significant loss of control incidents within 24 hours. While the Bill is not the right legislative framework to place duties on developers, where stronger protections are needed, we will act. Through recent amendments, the Bill will allow the Government to have a better understanding of significant loss of control incidents and how they are affecting essential services such as the NHS.

hansard.speaker: Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath (Lab)
hansard.text: On 10 November, the DfE launched a consultation on a safety certification framework for certain types of edtech used in education settings. The proposed approach focuses on products and features with the greatest potential to cause harm in three areas: serious data infringements, harmful content exposure and risks to cognitive development and social and emotional well-being. This includes products with certain gamification features. This will build on existing digital and technology standards and generative AI product safety standards. The consultation will help develop a proportionate and robust approach to help schools identify products meeting relevant safety expectations and to inform purchasing decisions.

hansard.debate: Financial Services and Markets Bill  [Lords]  (Fourth sitting)
hansard.speaker: Lucy Rigby

Members, if they have the opportunity, make a similar visit to a local bank or otherwise. It is worth doing for various reasons. It is so important that we combat fraud. hansard.speaker: Baroness Lloyd of Effra (Lab)
hansard.text: I pay tribute to the noble Lord's commitment and conviction that we must learn lessons from the Synnovis attack. That is exactly the right approach. We agree that robust data hygiene, through data minimisation and anonymisation, is vital for ensuring privacy and defending against cyber attacks. hansard.debate: Financial Services and Markets Bill  [Lords]  (Fourth sitting)
hansard.speaker: Bobby Dean
hansard.text: I will speak briefly. First, I thank hon. Members for their contributions; I appreciate their spirit and general support. There was a question about whether the new clause also applies to telecoms companies; it does. There was also a comment about the relevance of FCA regulators here. If the APP framework that is in place is not specifically a role for the FCA—although, it will always need to play a part in this—it is certainly an enhanced role for the Treasury. Things should not be left to DCMS and Ofcom. The framework places the liability on financial firms, and that is inherently unfair. We need to find a way to expand that framework to make tech companies directly liable. This is not about creating a generalised rule for the type of content that those companies allow on their platforms; the Online Safety Act focuses on that. If fines will be issued in the future, it will be because platforms have repeatedly failed to take down content that we deem to be illegal. That will be a more general measure, whereas we are trying to place direct liability on tech companies for instances of fraud. The APP framework already exists and is something we can build on. I hope this conversation can continue in the Treasury to create direct liability for individual cases, as has been experimented with in other jurisdictions, such as Australia. I will press the new clause to a Division. Question put , That the clause be read a Second time.

hansard.debate: Financial Services and Markets Bill  [Lords]  (Fourth sitting)
hansard.speaker: Sam Carling
hansard.text: I must admit that, until recently, I did not know a great deal about reimbursement and redress schemes for fraud victims, but that changed when I discovered earlier this month that a member of my own family had recently fallen victim to fraud and lost more than £30,000. Member for Mid Bedfordshire, I do not know that the FCA would have the jurisdiction to require reimbursement payments from technology companies, as the type of company in question is not usually FCA-regulated. hansard.debate: Financial Services and Markets Bill  [Lords]  (Third sitting)
hansard.speaker: Lauren Edwards
hansard.text: I support the clauses, but I take this opportunity to make the point that the regulators should continue to ensure that the statement of responsibilities is updated for significant changes and provided to the regulators. When I was a supervisor, newer risks such as cyber tended to change around within a firm's allocation of SMCR responsibilities. I suspect that is now likely the case for artificial intelligence. It is really important for business-as-usual supervision that supervisory teams always know who is on the hook if things go wrong, so that there can be speedy resolution. I am keen to ensure that AI is properly considered in the SMCR regime. hansard.debate: Financial Services and Markets Bill  [Lords]  (Third sitting)
hansard.speaker: Lucy Rigby
hansard.text: I welcome the shadow Economic Secretary's agreement with the broad thrust of these reforms. hansard.text: The noble Lord is right about the importance of the UK developing sovereign capabilities, but we must also have access to the right global capabilities. We want the UK, the NHS and others to benefit from the advances that we are seeing. In respect of our own developments, we have £500 million in our sovereign AI fund that is continuing to make investments, the £1.1 billion AI hardware plan and the £2 billion quantum investment, all of which are building out UK capabilities which will support the public and private sectors.

hansard.speaker: Baroness Lloyd of Effra (Lab)
hansard.text: My noble friend is absolutely right to draw attention to the considerable developments in AI, which are bringing huge opportunities. Yesterday, my noble friend the Minister for Health was talking about the EDITH trial in the NHS. There are huge developments, and they must be carefully and responsibly developed. We are taking that further through the cyber security and resilience Bill, and we will continue to act where needed.

hansard.speaker: Sarah Pochin (Runcorn and Helsby) (Reform)
hansard.text: T7. Scientists at the Daresbury laboratory in my constituency help British businesses harness the power of AI and supercomputing. hansard.speaker: Fred Thomas (Plymouth Moor View) (Lab)
hansard.text: When there is clear political and strategic direction from the Government around which technologies they want to invest in and back, we have the massive successes we have seen recently, not least through sovereign AI. hansard.speaker: Baroness in Waiting/Government Whip (Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath) (Lab)
hansard.text: Our approach to educational technology is underpinned by sector engagement and our research portfolio, which is published on GOV.UK. When used effectively alongside high-quality teaching, technology can improve outcomes, reduce workload and support inclusion. However, evidence about what works, for whom and in what circumstances remains limited. That is why we are strengthening the evidence base through the Technology in Schools survey, the £24 million EdTech Testbed programme and the AI Tutoring Tools Pioneers programme, alongside wider research partnerships.

hansard.debate: Creative Industries, Culture and the Arts
hansard.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, I congratulate my noble friends Lady McAnea, on her wonderful maiden speech, and Lady Caine, on her excellent introduction to this debate. She made a powerful case and, given the evidence, it is vital that we should protect the creative industries where they are under threat. This is inarguably the case with respect to the theft of creative content by AI companies. I sit on your Lordships' Communications and Digital Select Committee, which published a report on this issue earlier in the year. I will leave it to our chair, my noble friend Lady Keeley, to say more, but I urge the Government to move forward quickly on transparency and other measures to safeguard the livelihoods of content creators. Generative AI is also causing us to reflect on what it is to be human, as we did earlier this year in a debate led by the most reverend Primate the Archbishop of Canterbury. The arts are our expression of humanity: they tell our stories and delight in our inconsistencies. In the words of the John Legend song, the arts celebrate our “curves”, our “edges” and all our “perfect imperfections”. Younger people in particular appear to be pushing back against the mass-produced perfection of technology, craving the authenticity of live events and human connections, even as our addiction to social media algorithms corrodes our confidence to form those real-life relationships. The labour market is also changing fast in response to all this, and it is hard to predict what attributes will be valued in the future. However, I would put my money on our human skills being at a premium as technology gets better at everything else. In that context, I welcome the Government's rebalancing of the school curriculum to restore the importance of the arts, and I remind the House of my interests

hansard.debate: Creative Industries, Culture and the Arts
hansard.speaker: Lord Camoys (Con)

Britain is where the international creative sector wants to do business. We cannot be complacent. For UK-financed, and often smaller-budget, films, the picture is not so rosy. Part of ensuring continued investment in new domestic and international production is demonstrating that the UK has modern, state-of-the-art studios to deliver this work. hansard.debate: Creative Industries, Culture and the Arts
hansard.speaker: Lord Hampton (CB)
hansard.text: My Lords, like everyone here, I thank the noble Baroness, Lady Caine of Kentish Town, for this debate. Luckily enough, I have a friend who used to work in Singapore, the ridiculously talented Rajinder Singh, a painter, sculptor, choreographer and poet. I asked him, “Raj, what is the most creative place in the world?” He said, “What you get in London is, oh my God, it's everything. New York doesn't even come close”. That made me think: what is it about this small, drafty, crowded island that makes us so creative? Many countries, as we have heard, have tax breaks and incentives; they pay you to be artists. We almost go the other way. From school onwards, it is increasingly difficult to follow a creative path, and maybe that is the point. Harry Lime in “The Third Man”, the best film ever made—incidentally British—talks about how the 30 years of Borgia rule gave us the Renaissance. Let us face it: sometimes in the last 10 years it has felt like we are living under Borgia rule. hansard.speaker: Steve Reed (Streatham and Croydon North) (Lab/Co-op)
hansard.text: It is a pleasure to serve under your chairmanship, Dame Siobhain. I congratulate my hon. hansard.speaker: Lord Hall of Birkenhead (CB)
hansard.text: My Lords, I too congratulate the noble Baroness, Lady Caine—she is also my friend—on winning space for this important debate. If you had said to me 25 years ago that Cardiff would be a really important centre for production in the media, I would have thought it was a long shot. But the power of Doctor Who has sparked something quite remarkable: the Daleks do not just exterminate, they create jobs. Within five years of the BBC's construction of the studios at Roath Lock in Cardiff Bay in 2012, the number of creative firms that were registered or headquartered within a radius of 20 kilometres grew by 47%. That is extraordinary. Another example dear to my heart is the BBC in Salford, opened in 2012. Within five years, there was a 105% increase in creative firms registered or headquartered within 25 kilometres. The BBC creates creative clusters. hansard.debate: Creative Industries, Culture and the Arts
hansard.speaker: Lord Vaizey of Didcot (Con)

hansard.text: No particularly good reason springs to mind, to be perfectly honest. hansard.speaker: Charlie Dewhirst (Bridlington and The Wolds) (Con)
hansard.text: I thank the Minister for advance sight of his statement, and for the opportunity to see the documents earlier today. I join him in keeping the victims of Jeffrey Epstein at the front of our minds. They are owed the truth, and nine months after this House demanded the truth, it is still arriving in instalments. In January 2025, before Peter Mandelson set foot in Washington, the head of the Foreign Office asked the obvious question: unless Mandelson's Global Counsel shares could be sold immediately, when would they go into a blind trust? On 11 March, the right hon. Member for Bristol North West (Darren Jones) told the House that the rules required new civil servants to give up such interests before taking office—but seemingly not this one. In June 2025, a Foreign Office Minister told the House that there was a “robust and established process”; the permanent under-secretary's own phrase for it in these papers was “light touch”. Of course Wales stands to gain more from our steel fund, but to say that it has not got the money, Mr Speaker—

hansard.text: Perhaps I will not thank the shadow Minister for that question. If we are frank about the 14 years of Conservative Government, the economy was basically stagnant over that period, despite the fact that there was record immigration—it is actually quite hard to underperform that badly and for the economy to not develop when so many people are coming to the UK. Since the election, we have seen not only stronger economic growth, but stronger economic growth per capita, so people are really feeling the benefits. We have already signed an unbalanced and unfair deal, and it is a deal we cannot enforce. As the noble Lord, Lord Frost, said

hansard.speaker: Baroness Finn (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, I begin by congratulating the noble Lord, Lord Khan of Tooting, on such an inspiring and impressive maiden speech. I am sure we can look forward to many great future contributions from him in this House. I congratulate the noble Lord, Lord, Liddle, on securing this debate. I admired his customary elegance and eloquence as he relitigated so many arguments of the past. I count myself among the many noble Lords who bore witness to the many years of painstaking effort required to implement the will of the British people, as expressed in the referendum of 2016, to leave the European Union. It took more than four and a half years to bring that process to its conclusion. Now, the Prime Minister, through a combination of gradual backsliding on our sovereign rights and through repeated hints that he wishes to take the United Kingdom back into the European Union, appears intent on subjecting the country to many more years of uncertainty and division—what my noble friend Lord Saatchi referred to as the eternal nightmare of arguments about Europe. The Prime Minister's approach has drawn criticism from no fewer than six of his predecessors. Even Sir Tony Blair, one of Europe's most ardent advocates, has warned that the European Union is moving in the wrong direction on technological regulation. What is the Prime Minister's response? He tells us that he will not be listening to those voices. He will not listen to his predecessors, and he appears equally unwilling to heed the verdict of the 17 million people who voted to leave the European Union. It is hard to disagree with my noble friend Lady May of Maidenhead; she is correct that the Prime Minister should accept Brexit and move on. hansard.speaker: Baroness Bennett of Manor Castle (GP)

I want to add another foundational contribution to that list: the place of creative thinking, and the creation of art and craft, in solving the polycrisis that our species now faces in tackling our currently terribly limited understanding of our own bodies, ecosystems, the earth's systems and our narrow ideas about economies and societies. hansard.debate: Financial Services and Markets Bill  [Lords]  (Third sitting)
hansard.speaker: Lucy Rigby
hansard.text: Effective recovery powers are essential if law enforcement is to address the growing use of cryptoassets by criminals. Clause 49 introduces a targeted delegated power to update existing cryptoasset recovery powers through secondary legislation, where that is necessary to ensure that they continue to operate effectively. This will enable the cryptoasset recovery regime to keep pace with developments in technology and business models, without the need for primary legislation each time a change is required. As we all know, money laundering undermines legitimate businesses, distorts competition and funds organised crime. The latest national risk assessment on money laundering and terrorist financing shows a growing use of cryptoassets to launder criminal proceeds, including for sanctions evasion, ransomware and theft, posing a significant threat to the UK. We strengthened powers to recover illicit cryptoassets through the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023, and those powers have been used successfully. However, the rapid evolution of cryptoasset technology and markets means that practical gaps have emerged in how the legislation operates. In particular, the current crypto-wallet freezing order regime is limited by aspects of the definitions used, including the definition of “UK nexus” being used in ways that were not foreseen. In some circumstances, law enforcement can identify and even freeze illicit assets but cannot recover them. I have spoken to law enforcement in other jurisdictions where these powers are available, and I have been told just how important the powers are to recovering illicit cryptoassets in an impactful way. hansard.speaker: Sam Carling
hansard.text: I do not disagree with hon. Gentleman. Even just a few years ago, the main anti-fraud warnings were often based on email fraud. Now that has changed to social media and telephones. It is an evolving situation. He makes a valuable point. We desperately need joined-up regulation. City of London police data shows that courier fraud continues to rise, with more than £21 million scammed from people in 2025. The despicable people who carry it out prey especially on vulnerable older people, with 62% of reports coming from people aged 76 to 96.

hansard.debate: Financial Services and Markets Bill  [Lords]  (Fourth sitting)
hansard.speaker: Lauren Edwards
hansard.text: The Minister will probably not support the new clause, but I ask her to use her influence to develop a specific strategy to tackle APP fraud—if not in the Bill, then somewhere else. We need to find a way of capturing the role of social media companies in stopping APP fraud, and of making them play their part in sharing costs with the banks, which can only do so much to tackle it. The cost to the economy is huge. Back in 2024—I cited this on Second Reading, but let me do so again—the estimated cost of APP fraud was somewhere in the region of £450 million. That is considerable, and we really need to crack down on it. I ask the Minister to consider whether another mechanism could bring forward a strategy to tackle such a significant harm.

hansard.text: First, I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Barking (Nesil Caliskan) for securing this debate. It is a really important debate, and I am really pleased to be able to contribute to it during Islamophobia Awareness Month. I have spent years working alongside women from the Muslim communities in Camden, where I serve, and I have seen at first hand the enormous contribution that they make to our communities and the discrimination that they continue to face. I have heard from women who experience anti-Muslim abuse on the street, on public transport, in their workplaces and when simply going about their daily lives. We have to recognise that Islamophobia is increasingly also an issue of misogyny and sexism. For many women, their faith is immediately visible, and that visibility can make them particularly vulnerable. There is a deeply troubling intersection between hatred of Muslims and the desire to intimidate, humiliate and control women because of how they look, what they wear and what they believe. What concerns me deeply is not just the increase in hate and hostility, but the growing sense of resignation that many women feel, which sits really well alongside the theme of this debate. They tell me that they do not want to report any incidents anymore, because they do not believe that anything will be done and because the process of reporting can feel like another burden to bear, rather than a route to justice. This is an incredibly troubling place for our community to find itself. No one should feel that Islamophobia is simply an accepted part of everyday life. hansard.debate: Creative Industries, Culture and the Arts
hansard.speaker: Lord Storey (LD)
hansard.text: My Lords, a big thank you to the noble Baroness, Lady Caine, for initiating this important debate and for her stirring speech. The mantra of the Government is, quite rightly, growth. How interesting it is that the last set of figures showed that the creative industries' GVA grew by 4.6%—more than four times the 1% of the wider UK economy. I will start with a success story that has already been mentioned. Last week saw the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. Originally created by a British team before expanding into a global, multi-studio operation, this now American-owned company has staggering profits. In the UK, it has its headquarters in the city of Edinburgh, with studios in London, Leeds and Lincoln. Yet, for all the success of the creative industries, there are a number of issues that need government action and support, some of which have been mentioned. They include undercapitalisation; the skills gap and workforce retention; intellectual property and the protection of creators' rights; and declining funding and support for creative subjects in schools and higher education. There is also a need to tackle the lack of regional opportunities for the creative industries, with London and the south-east being dominant for most of the creatives. Public service broadcast plays a huge part in fostering and developing opportunities for the creative industries. However, with Channel 5 now being owned by Paramount, Sky by Comcast, and Sky bidding to take over ITV, that will leave us with only two UK-owned PSBs: Channel 4 and the BBC. hansard.speaker: Mark Garnier
hansard.text: That is a really important point. We have spoken at great length in this Committee about how the regulators are being flexible and are getting on with it, but what is our long-term goal? What is our north star when it comes to this stuff? That is the most important point, because other countries around the world do have a north star and are showing where they are trying to get to. When people invest in this type of stuff, they want long-term certainty. Weirdly, the hon. Gentleman raises—without intending to—another really important point, which is that the UK is an unbelievably good incubator of this type of stuff. We see companies setting up here and getting seed funding and series A funding, but they leave and go to other countries, where they get B and C, and then a listing. There are a whole load of reasons why that is going on, and we are trying to understand what is behind it, but the bottom line is that we are great at starting these things, but we are not going forward. If we have a strategy and people know what our north star is, then they will get behind it and understand where it is going and what the opportunity is. There are also other issues. I have already referenced this, albeit rather obliquely, but it is really important—it refers back to a point we were discussing this morning. I think we all want regulation—not simply in relation to the ringfence, but more broadly—to be appropriate and proportionate. For all those reasons, we are bringing forward these reforms. hansard.debate: Peter Mandelson:  Response to Humble Address
hansard.speaker: John McDonnell (Hayes and Harlington) (Lab)
hansard.text: I have tried to trawl through the list of information provided today, but could I ask the Minister about the completeness of that information? He will know that there were concerns across the House during this episode when we were told that Morgan McSweeney's phone was lost. A subsequent FOI request was submitted by an individual, and I have the Information Commissioner's decision in front of me. It was discovered that, although this phone was lost or stolen, a number of messages were retained that could have been made available, but the Government refused to allow them to be released, because they were described as official information. The Information Commissioner decided that they should be released, and I believe the deadline is close to being up. Could the Minister advise me whether the information provided today covers all that information and does it comply with the Information Commissioner's judgment? If not, when will the other elements of those messages be released? From what we understand, they relate to the advice, some of which is published today, of Peter Mandelson to Morgan McSweeney about the Cabinet reshuffle. Could I also ask which Minister took the decision not to release this information, when it was quite clear that in many ways it was not official business, but could readily have been released to inform the House?

hansard.speaker: Josh Newbury (Cannock Chase) (Lab)
hansard.text: I congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett) on securing this debate and on her fantastic work on the brilliant “Yes, sex please! We're British!” campaign; I thank her for it too. She has been rightly bold in knocking down some of the barriers that have historically surrounded conversations about sex, sexual health and relationships. Her work on the issue has been groundbreaking and stigma-breaking, and that should be warmly welcomed in all quarters. I have to say that I have been deeply disappointed to see some of the coverage of my hon. Friend's work in the media, particularly the reductive nature of some responses, reducing what is an important and serious campaign to nicknames like “the sex MP” or a juvenile obsession with the suggestion that sex toys might be brought into Portcullis House, as if they are something shameful or inappropriate that should not be brought into a place like this, where we can and should debate all aspects of our health and wellbeing. The fact that some people see fit to try to ridicule a strong woman standing up in Parliament and talking openly about sexual health and education proves exactly the point that she is trying to make. We should encourage such conversations, not make people feel embarrassed or uncomfortable for having them. As I shared with the House on last year's International Men's Day, I have my own experience of spiking and sexual assault. It was a difficult thing to speak about publicly, but what struck me afterwards was the response. hansard.debate: Financial Services and Markets Bill  [Lords]  (Fourth sitting)
hansard.speaker: The Economic Secretary to the Treasury (Lucy Rigby)
hansard.text: It is an honour to serve under your chairship, Mrs Hobhouse. I will explain why the clause should not stand part of the Bill, but first I will explain Government new clause 18 and Government amendment 35. The debate on digital assets in the other place indicated that legislative and regulatory change is required to facilitate digital assets. The Government have also heard that message clearly from the wholesale digital markets champion and taskforce—they are doing important work. The Government agree that further action is necessary. The UK's legal and regulatory system is generally considered sufficiently broad and adaptable to enable digital markets to scale in the UK. Where it is not, and where the Government want to test changes to encourage innovation, the Government have designed the digital securities sandbox—using the financial market infrastructure or FMI sandbox powers under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023—to adapt legislation and regulation. In some areas, however, additional certainty is needed to maintain market momentum, and where proposals do not need to be tested in a sandbox. Those could include areas where our policy intent is the same as existing legislation, but we want to enable that activity to be done using new technology—for example in relation to the legal basis for the ownership and transfer of financial assets. Dealing with such references in legislation is particularly important to support the work of the wholesale digital markets champion. If there were references in legislation that do not support digital assets adoption, and those could not be amended quickly, that would undermine the efforts of the champion and of the wider market to deploy digital assets at scale. The issue has previously been raised as part of the debate on

hansard.speaker: Ms Billington
hansard.text: I agree with the right hon. Gentleman and I am grateful to him for raising that issue. The situation for people off grid who are reliant on heating oil has been very bad for a long time. I am pleased that we have finally agreed to regulate the heating oil market, on the recommendation of the Competition and Markets Authority, and we will work at pace to get that right. In the interim, we have allocated £53 million to local authorities and the devolved Administrations, to ensure that people can access some kind of support. I have said this before at the Dispatch Box and I will say it again: anyone in a local authority who is administering that crisis and resilience fund should be aware that I am keen for that money to get out the door. We have already started to have freezing temperatures this winter, and people on heating oil in particular must make sure that they get that help.

hansard.speaker: Adrian Ramsay (Waveney Valley) (Green)
hansard.text: The Leader of the House will have heard that the Competition and Markets Authority today released a report showing that patients are getting a bad deal from private sector dentistry. In too many cases, companies are charging increasingly high costs, selling unnecessary expensive treatments and pressing NHS patients to go private. We have seen slow progress from this Government, so can the Leader of the House tell us when they will make a statement on the long-promised consultation to reform the dental contract, and whether we will have a debate in this House on restoring NHS dentistry?

hansard.speaker: Helen Maguire (Epsom and Ewell) (LD)
hansard.text: A Competition and Markets Authority report published today confirmed in black and white how broken the dental market is. It says that 4 million people did not go to the dentist in the past two years due to the cost. Quite frankly, this is a cost of living and healthcare scandal, and it has seen people driven into debt and pulling out their own teeth. Will the Leader of the House consider a debate on the merits of a dental rescue package, which would guarantee NHS dentistry for everyone, opening treatment centres for those with urgent needs and cutting prices?

hansard.speaker: Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath (Lab)
hansard.text: As my noble friend said, technology used purposefully as part of high-quality teaching is important for a number of subjects and qualifications, including computing, and can support the practical applied learning we want every child to experience, including the new vocational GCSEs. Good implementation matters. We will fund the National Centre for Computing Education, providing world-class CPD for teachers, and will work with schools and the sector to provide appropriate resources, guidance, professional development and access to specialist expertise and facilities.
